Stated Claim / Post Context:
Could lifting the Roadless Rule drive a logging boom in the Tongass?

According to the U.S. Forest Service, 188,000 acres of currently roadless land could be considered suitable for logging in the Tongass under the current Forest Management Plan if the road ban dissolves. That would be less than 2% of the Tongass.

Actual Article Body:
For decades, the Roadless Rule banned new roadbuilding and logging across millions of acres of national forest land. The Trump Administration has moved to lift the ban, and that’s controversial in Alaska’s Tongass National Forest, the largest national forest in the U.S.

Around half of the Tongass in Southeast Alaska has no active roads, an area spanning more than 9 million acres.

On a recent afternoon, Judith Dax̱ootsú Ramos walked through a roadless area on Douglas Island. She’s a Lingít anthropologist from Yakutat, a small Alaska Native village, and said the forest supports Lingit traditions, including harvesting berries and hunting deer.

“Without this, we’re going to lose our traditional medicines, our traditional art styles, our traditional foods, and all that is really connected to the forest,” Ramos said.

Ramos sits on the board of the Southeast Alaska Conservation Council, a local nonprofit advocating to keep the Roadless Rule in place. The board visited Prince of Wales Island, a heavily logged part of the forest. Ramos said the trees that grew back in old-growth clear cuts looked sterile.

“It’s a very different forest, and there was no animals, no birds there, and it was kind of really quiet, and so it was kind of scary,” she said.

The Lingít have lived in the region that is now the Tongass for at least 10,000 years. Ramos said it’s important to protect the forest so people can live here long into the future.

“We can’t ignore that our climate is changing,” Ramos said. “We need an intact forest system.”

The Tongass National Forest is a carbon sink. It holds a third of all carbon stored in intact U.S. national forests, according to research published in the scientific journal AGU Advances.

The Roadless Rule has been rolled back and reinstated multiple times since the U.S. Department of Agriculture established it to protect forestlands in 2001. Retaining the rule has drawn broad public support each time it’s been on the chopping block.

[Source 2 — alaskapublic.org (Bias: Independent / Unrated)] (URL: https://alaskapublic.org/news/environment/2026-11-06/could-lifting-the-roadless-rule-drive-a-logging-boom-in-the-tongass):
“When we have the back and forth on a four-year cycle — it doesn’t matter which side — it creates so many challenges for our communities,” she said.

Susan Alexander is a retired Forest Service economist who worked in the Tongass.

She said when the Roadless Rule has flip-flopped under past administrations, getting rid of it didn’t ramp up logging in the Tongass. But she said it did prompt the Forest Service to prepare timber sales that never sold. [...] This time, the U.S. Department of Agriculture has said that it wants to roll back the Roadless Rule nationwide to give firefighters access to fight wildfires and remove regulatory barriers. In this part of Alaska, where wildfires are rare, many think that’s an excuse to bolster the timber industry, which has declined significantly since the 1990s.

But could the move stimulate a logging boom in the Tongass? [...] ### Loggable land

According to the U.S.Forest Service, 188,000 acres of currently roadless land could be considered suitable for logging in the Tongass under the current Forest Management Plan if the road ban dissolves. That would be less than 2% of the Tongass. Roughly 4% of the forest has already been logged.
